title: Fitbit Charge 3 oxygen-variation signals precede COVID-19 exacerbation in 4 of 5 cases and reveal severe sleep apnoea in one patient (DEXTERITY pilot, Kanazawa)
summary: Kanazawa pilot, 23 COVID-19 patients (2020): Fitbit oxygen-variation signals preceded 4 of 5 exacerbations (sensitivity 80%); one man's persistent signals led to polysomnography showing severe OSAS.
account: Yamagami, Nomura and colleagues published the DEXTERITY pilot in JMIR Formative Research on 16 September 2021. They are at Kanazawa University and Japan Community Health Care Organization (JCHO) Kanazawa Hospital. The study ran from August to November 2020. The individual event is undated. Twenty-three patients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 wore a Fitbit Charge 3 for 30 days. The investigators defined a high “estimated oxygen variation” (EOV) signal as a significant dip and recovery of the oxygen level within the index period. A prediction counted as successful if the signal appeared within two days before an exacerbation. Exacerbation occurred in six patients (seven events). EOV signals preceded four of five analyzed cases (sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%), better than resting-heart-rate signals (50% and 80%). Separately, patient JCHO-023, a 53-year-old man with hypertension recovered from COVID-19, showed “a long-lasting high EOV signal” from days 18 to 29 without symptoms. The team suspected sleep apnea. A portable polysomnogram (Nihon Kohden SAS-2200) gave a 3% oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 33.6 per hour, severe obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. The paper reports no treatment for him. The authors note the Fitbit's functions and analysis algorithms were not approved as a medical device at the time. They note that baseline data were short and the five exacerbation cases are too few to generalize. The prediction analysis was defined against outcomes after the fact rather than as live alerts.
purpose: Fitbit's EOV metric summarizes overnight oxygen variation for consumers. The investigators repurposed it to flag COVID-19 deterioration, and the sleep-apnea finding was incidental to that study aim.
system: Fitbit Charge 3 estimated oxygen variation (EOV) and resting heart rate, with investigator-defined signal thresholds
developer: Fitbit (device and EOV algorithm); Kanazawa University investigators (signal definitions)
deployer: Kanazawa University and JCHO Kanazawa Hospital (DEXTERITY pilot, UMIN000041421)

ratings.reason: One man received a diagnosis of severe obstructive sleep apnea (3% ODI 33.6/h) from an incidental wearable signal. The paper reports no treatment or follow-up for him.
The 80% sensitivity for predicting exacerbation is a retrospective pilot result on five events, which the authors say is too small to generalize. No live alerting or changed care is documented.

ai_role.statement: The device produced the EOV values. The investigators' own rule flagged high signals, and clinicians decided to order polysomnography for the sleep-apnea patient. The paper does not say whether Fitbit's EOV estimation uses machine learning and notes the functions were not approved as a medical device. The COVID-19 prediction figures were computed after the outcomes were known, not from alerts acted on in real time.

fields.account: Yamagami, Nomura and colleagues published the DEXTERITY pilot in JMIR Formative Research on 16 September 2021. They are at Kanazawa University and Japan Community Health Care Organization (JCHO) Kanazawa Hospital. The study ran from August to November 2020. The individual event is undated. Twenty-three patients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 wore a Fitbit Charge 3 for 30 days. The investigators defined a high “estimated oxygen variation” (EOV) signal as a significant dip and recovery of the oxygen level within the index period. A prediction counted as successful if the signal appeared within two days before an exacerbation. Exacerbation occurred in six patients (seven events). EOV signals preceded four of five analyzed cases (sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%), better than resting-heart-rate signals (50% and 80%). Separately, patient JCHO-023, a 53-year-old man with hypertension recovered from COVID-19, showed “a long-lasting high EOV signal” from days 18 to 29 without symptoms. The team suspected sleep apnea. A portable polysomnogram (Nihon Kohden SAS-2200) gave a 3% oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 33.6 per hour, severe obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. The paper reports no treatment for him. The authors note the Fitbit's functions and analysis algorithms were not approved as a medical device at the time. They note that baseline data were short and the five exacerbation cases are too few to generalize. The prediction analysis was defined against outcomes after the fact rather than as live alerts.

fields.account: Yamagami, Nomura and colleagues published the DEXTERITY pilot in JMIR Formative Research on 16 September 2021. They are at Kanazawa University and Japan Community Health Care Organization (JCHO) Kanazawa Hospital. The study ran from August to November 2020. The individual event is undated. Twenty-three patients with PCR-confirmed COVID-19 wore a Fitbit Charge 3 for 30 days. The investigators defined a high “estimated oxygen variation” (EOV) signal as a significant dip and recovery of the oxygen level within the index period. A prediction counted as successful if the signal appeared within two days before an exacerbation. Exacerbation occurred in six patients (seven events). EOV signals preceded four of five analyzed cases (sensitivity 80%, specificity 90%), better than resting-heart-rate signals (50% and 80%). Separately, patient JCHO-023, a 53-year-old man with hypertension recovered from COVID-19, showed “a long-lasting high EOV signal” from days 18 to 29 without symptoms. The team suspected sleep apnea. A portable polysomnogram (Nihon Kohden SAS-2200) gave a 3% oxygen desaturation index (ODI) of 33.6 per hour, severe obstructive sleep apnea syndrome. The paper reports no treatment for him. The authors note the Fitbit's functions and analysis algorithms were not approved as a medical device at the time. They note that baseline data were short and the five exacerbation cases are too few to generalize. The prediction analysis was defined against outcomes after the fact rather than as live alerts.
